Apple has filed its opposition to a motion to dismiss the lawsuit submitted by OpenAI. The lawsuit accuses two former Apple employees, along with OpenAI and io Products, of stealing its trade secrets. Here are the details.

A little background

A few days ago, OpenAI filed a motion to dismiss the lawsuit brought by Apple, which accused OpenAI, io Products, Chang Liu, and Tang Tan of trade secret theft.

In the request, OpenAI stated that Apple filed the lawsuit "without a sufficient investigation" and further presented its version of the events that led Apple to file suit.

OpenAI's rebuttal centers on three main arguments: that Apple "failed to allege ownership of protectable trade secrets," "failed to allege conduct sufficient to support a misappropriation claim," and "failed to reasonably allege any damage or ongoing harm."

OpenAI claims that, contrary to Apple's allegations, former Apple employee Chang Liu was consulted by a former colleague after his departure, rather than accessing Apple materials without authorization; while former Apple vice president Tang Tan retained Apple's offboarding documents to ensure new hires complied with its security procedures.

The company also argued that Apple's own information management and offboarding practices bear some responsibility, claiming the company encouraged employees to use personal iCloud accounts for work and did not properly cut off departing employees' access to company materials.

"Apple's complaint concerns specific individuals stealing specific Apple trade secrets in specific ways"

Today, Apple filed its opposition to OpenAI's motion to dismiss, breaking down OpenAI's rebuttal arguments point by point and stating that "in short, defendants do not confront the alarming allegations at the core of the complaint."

Apple argues that its original complaint "adequately identifies the specific trade secrets allegedly misappropriated by defendants," citing precedent for courts finding a similar level of detail sufficient to allow trade secret claims to proceed.

Apple also said OpenAI's claim that it inadequately protected its trade secrets was "equally unavailing," and that OpenAI "dismisses Apple's trade secrets as mere 'supplier relationships' and then questions whether all 'supplier relationships' are confidential."

Apple further argued that OpenAI is misusing the motion to dismiss mechanism wholesale. The documents read:

In its opposition, Apple also directly addressed a heavily redacted transcript of a conversation that OpenAI made public on its website, involving a former colleague still working at Apple reaching out to Chang Liu to clarify some information about an Apple project.

OpenAI argued that the conversation proved Apple's characterization of Liu's post-departure access to materials as theft was misleading, because Apple's own employees had reached out to him themselves to retrieve information.
